danish.title: Femtende bog (1812–13) — Kapitel 11
paragraphs: Næste dag gav feltmarskalken middag og bal, som kejseren ærede med sin nærværelse. Kutuzov havde modtaget Sankt Georgs-ordenen af Første Klasse, og kejseren viste ham de højeste æresbevisninger, men alle vidste, at kejseren var utilfreds med ham. Etikettten blev overholdt, og det var kejseren, der gik foran med eksemplet, men alle forstod, at den gamle mand var skyldig og ubrugelig. Da Kutuzov i overensstemmelse med en skik fra Katarinas tid befalede, at de erobrede standarter skulle sænkes for kejserens fødder, da han trådte ind i balsalen, trak kejseren på munden og mumlede noget, hvori nogle opfangede ordene »den gamle komediespiller«.
Kejserens mishag med Kutuzov blev især forstærket i Vilna af det forhold, at Kutuzov tydeligvis ikke kunne eller ikke ville forstå betydningen af det kommende felttog.
Da kejseren næste morgen sagde til de forsamlede officerer: »I har ikke blot reddet Rusland, I har reddet Europa!« forstod alle, at krigen ikke var slut.

Kutuzov alene ville ikke indse dette og udtalte åbent sin mening om, at ingen ny krig kunne forbedre Ruslands stilling eller øge dets hæder, men kun ville fordærve og forringe den glorværdige position, Rusland havde opnået. Han forsøgte at bevise for kejseren, at det var umuligt at udskrive nye tropper, talte om de lidelser, folket allerede havde gennemgået, om muligheden for fiasko og så videre.
Eftersom dette var feltmarskallens indstilling, blev han naturligt betragtet som blot en hindring og en forhindring for den forestående krig.

For at undgå ubehagelige sammenstød med den gamle mand var den naturlige metode at gøre det samme, som var gjort med ham ved Austerlitz og med Barclay i begyndelsen af det russiske felttog — nemlig overføre myndigheden til kejseren selv og derved trække tæppet væk under den øverstkommanderendes fødder uden at krænke den gamle mand ved at underrette ham om ændringen.

Med dette for øje blev hans stab gradvist omstruktureret, og dens virkelige styrke fjernet og overført til kejseren. Toll, Konovnitsyn og Jermolov fik nye udnævnelser. Alle talte højt om feltmarskallens store svækkelse og svigtende helbred.
Hans helbred måtte være dårligt, for at hans plads kunne overtages af en anden. Og hans helbred var virkelig dårligt.

Så naturligt, enkelt og gradvist — præcis som han var kommet fra Tyrkiet til skatkammeret i Petersborg for at hverve militsen, og derfra til hæren, da man havde brug for ham dér — nu da hans rolle var udspillet, blev Kutuzovs plads indtaget af en ny og nødvendig aktør.
Krigen i 1812, der foruden sin nationale betydning, der var kær for ethvert russisk hjerte, nu skulle antage en anden, europæisk, betydning.

Folkenes bevægelse fra vest mod øst skulle efterfølges af en folkebevægelse fra øst mod vest, og til denne nye krig var der brug for en anden leder med egenskaber og synspunkter, der afveg fra Kutuzovs, og som var drevet af andre motiver.
Alexander den Første var lige så nødvendig for folkenes bevægelse fra øst mod vest og for de nationale grænsers genfastsættelse, som Kutuzov havde været for Ruslands frelse og hæder.

Kutuzov forstod ikke, hvad Europa, magtbalancen eller Napoleon betød. Han kunne ikke forstå det. For repræsentanten for det russiske folk var der, efter at fjenden var tilintetgjort og Rusland befriet og hævet til toppunktet af sin hæder, intet mere at gøre som russer. Repræsentanten for den nationale krig havde intet andet tilbage end at dø, og Kutuzov døde.

english.title: Book Fifteen (1812 - 13) — Chapter 11
paragraphs: The next day the field marshal gave a dinner and ball that the Emperor honored with his presence. Kutuzov had received the Order of St. George, First Class, and the Emperor showed him the highest honors, but everyone knew of the imperial displeasure. The forms were observed and the Emperor was the first to set the example, yet everybody understood that the old man was considered at fault and good for nothing. When Kutuzov, following an old tradition from Catherine's day, ordered the captured standards lowered at the Emperor's feet as he entered the ballroom, the Emperor made a face and muttered something in which some people caught the words "the old comedian."
The Emperor's displeasure with Kutuzov was especially heightened at Vilna by the fact that Kutuzov clearly could not or would not understand the importance of the coming campaign.
When the Emperor told the assembled officers the following morning: "You have not only saved Russia, you have saved Europe!" they all understood that the war was not over.

Kutuzov alone refused to see this and openly stated that no new war could improve Russia's position or add to her glory, but could only diminish the glorious standing Russia had won. He tried to demonstrate to the Emperor the impossibility of raising fresh troops, spoke of the hardships the people had already endured, of the possibility of failure, and so on.
Given the field marshal's frame of mind, he was naturally regarded as nothing more than a hindrance and obstacle to the impending war.

To avoid unpleasant confrontations with the old man, the natural solution was to do what had been done with him at Austerlitz and with Barclay at the start of the Russian campaign: transfer authority to the Emperor himself, thus pulling the rug from under the commander in chief without upsetting the old man by telling him directly.

To this end, his staff was gradually restructured and its real power removed and transferred to the Emperor. Toll, Konovnitsyn, and Ermolov received new appointments. Everyone spoke openly of the field marshal's great weakness and failing health.
His health had to be bad for his position to be taken from him and given to another. And indeed his health was poor.

So naturally, simply, and gradually—just as he had come from Turkey to Petersburg to recruit the militia, and then to the army when he was needed—now that his part was played, Kutuzov's place was taken by a new and necessary performer.
The war of 1812, besides its national significance dear to every Russian heart, was now to take on another, European significance.

The movement of peoples from west to east was to be followed by a movement from east to west, and for this new war another leader was needed—one with different qualities and views, driven by different motives.
Alexander I was as necessary for the movement of peoples from east to west and for the redrawing of national boundaries as Kutuzov had been for the salvation and glory of Russia.

Kutuzov did not understand what Europe, the balance of power, or Napoleon meant. He could not understand it. For the representative of the Russian people, after the enemy had been destroyed and Russia had been liberated and raised to the summit of her glory, there was nothing left to do as a Russian. Nothing remained for the representative of the national war but to die. And Kutuzov died.
